reason: The objective is interpretive argument: show how an image carries a tone by citing the words that produce it. The evidence is the text itself, and the reasoning move is re-reading one line, holding a literal and a figurative construal together, and testing a tone word against them. Animation would compete for attention with the words and would dramatise a single mood, which is precisely the claim the case says must not be made ('no single correct feeling'); a static annotated page keeps the line, both readings and the evidence visible together while the learner argues.
staticAlternative: One annotated page with a four-line excerpt, for example 'The fog comes / on little cat feet. / It sits looking / over harbor and city' (Sandburg). The poem sits in the centre; the left margin holds a literal gloss (fog arrives and covers the harbour) and the right margin holds the figurative reading (soft, silent, watchful arrival), each tied to specific words by leader lines: 'little cat feet' for silence and lightness, 'sits looking' for stillness and attention, 'over' for quiet dominance. Below, a tone-evidence table with three candidate tone words (tender, watchful, unsettling) and an empty evidence column, so the learner must write the quoted words that support the tone they choose. A closing note distinguishes metaphor from irony and says two readers may defend different tone words if both cite the text.
